lesson.grammar_point: phrasal verbs for processes and decisions

listenings.text: Every week, a client calls me with the same question: do we need to stop using artificial intelligence until the new law is ready? My answer is no. Nobody is going to rule out AI in business. But you need to carry out a simple review now. First, find out where you use automated decisions, for example in credit or in hiring. Second, check if a person can look into a decision when a customer complains. And third, draw up a short internal policy. The watchdogs are not waiting for the new law, so neither should you.

I am not against regulation, but I am worried about how it is being drawn up. Lawmakers spend three years writing a law, and in those three years the technology changes completely. When the rules are finally phased in, they describe systems that nobody uses anymore. My suggestion is simple. Instead of long lists of prohibited technologies, set out clear principles, and let the agencies update the details every year. If the law cannot keep up with the technology, at least the regulator can.

reading.rtitle: Writing Rules for a Moving Target
paras: Every few months, a new breakthrough in artificial intelligence changes what the technology can do. For lawmakers, this creates a difficult problem: how do you write rules for something that is changing faster than the law? In most countries, the answer so far has been to regulate the uses of the technology, not the technology itself. A rule that describes one algorithm today may be useless next year.

Europe was one of the first regions to draw up a complete law. It sets out different levels of risk, from systems that are almost free to use to systems that are completely banned. The obligations are being phased in over several years, so that companies have time to adapt. Other countries, including Brazil, are discussing their own versions, and many governments have ruled out a single global model.

Critics say that no law can keep up with the technology, and that the real power is with a small number of large companies. Supporters answer that rules are not meant to stop innovation, but to make it safer. In the meantime, data protection watchdogs are already carrying out investigations and looking into complaints, using laws that were written before most people had heard of artificial intelligence.
